talks.title: Beyond the Horizon: Innovative Approaches to Space Cyberattack Scenarios
talks.teaser: Introduces a scenario-generation framework for space cyberattacks and walks through examples beyond jamming and spoofing.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a concern that public discussion of space cyber risk leans on a few stock stories, mostly jamming and spoofing. The speakers describe an NSF-funded study that brought together cyber specialists, aerospace engineers, space lawyers, ethicists and science fiction authors to imagine less obvious attacks. They stress how much daily life depends on satellites for navigation, communications, timing and weather monitoring, and they recall the 2022 Viasat disruption as a real example of a space-linked outage.

The middle section covers what makes the attack surface grow. Crowded orbits, aging hardware, weak security in small research satellites, long development cycles and decades-old space law all came up. The team presented the ICARUS matrix, a threat-modelling grid that combines threat actors, motivations, technical means and affected victims. Choosing one entry from each axis yields a scenario, which can then be checked with aerospace and cyber experts. Emerging technologies such as AI, autonomy and in-orbit robotics add further risk, with examples including data poisoning of Earth-observation classifiers and attacks on remote industrial platforms.

The closing part walks through example scenarios, such as an environmentally motivated actor interfering with wildfire monitoring. The speakers point to educational competitions as a way for newcomers to start learning. The practical takeaway is to treat space systems as cyber-physical systems, build scenarios with mixed expertise, and look past jamming when assessing risk.

talks.title: Evasion, Persistence, and Blinding EDR - Oh My
talks.teaser: Shows how AutoHotkey scripts slip past EDR tools and how defenders can detect and block them.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with the origin of AutoPwnKey, a framework the presenters built after malware families moved from AutoIt to AutoHotkey. They explain why AutoHotkey is hard for endpoint tools to judge: its interpreter carries a valid signature, it can run portably in user context without installation, and its scripts look like ordinary automation. They also outline how EDR products hook functions in system DLLs and how removing those hooks from ntdll can hide calls from monitoring.

The middle of the session is a series of live demos. These cover agent-to-server command execution, PowerShell run through Winget, an ntdll unhook followed by bulk file encryption and decryption, RDP-based lateral movement, a keylogger module, a UAC bypass, and a weaponized Excel document. A domain enumeration module checks for unconstrained delegation. The presenters report that most tested products missed many of these actions, while one tested host was eventually detected and contained after an alert.

The closing section focuses on defense. AutoHotkey loads far more DLLs than a typical process, so import counts are a useful signal. The presenters recommend baselining where the tool is used, blocking the interpreter where it is not needed, writing custom indicators of attack, restricting sensor traffic with host firewall rules, and applying application control, since the framework needs no admin rights to run.

talks.title: Alice & Bob Lose Their Life Savings
talks.teaser: Traces a real tech-support scam that drained a retired couple's savings and shows how a trusted-contact habit can stop it.
talks.summary:
Chad Butler walks through the true story of two retired Arizona residents, called Alice and Bob here, who lost nearly $300,000 in a tech-support scam. It began with a fake Microsoft warning on Alice's computer. A caller posing as a federal investigator then told her that her identity was linked to a criminal case and that her accounts would be frozen unless she moved her money. Over several weeks she withdrew cash, mailed it in a box, bought gold bullion for couriers to collect at her curb, and sent funds through a Bitcoin ATM.

Butler breaks down the script: the coached answers for the bank, the secrecy demands, and the pressure that kept her from asking for help. A shipping clerk recognized the address, and the mailed cash was eventually returned, but the scam only fell apart when the caller stopped answering scheduled calls. Police took a report but had little capacity to investigate. Citing FTC data, he notes that people under 60 file more of these reports than older adults, even though older victims lose more per incident. He argues that fear, urgency and authority override rational thinking in anyone.

He introduces the "Gumby Challenge," a habit of talking a suspicious request through with a trusted person before sending money, and asks listeners to be that trusted contact for relatives and friends. He closes with local nonprofit and FTC resources for education and victim support.

talks.title: How Generative AI is Shaping Online Threats
talks.teaser: Shows how generative AI is changing influence operations, harassment and child-safety abuse, using takedown and threat-report data.
talks.summary:
Shelby Grossman of the Stanford Cyber Policy Center asks whether generative AI has changed what online threats look like or only how cheaply they are produced. She defines covert influence operations as coordinated efforts to mislead, where the deception often sits in the account rather than the content. Comparing older campaigns with AI-era reports from model providers, she finds familiar narratives. A survey experiment found AI-written propaganda slightly less persuasive than human-written propaganda, but about as persuasive once a person edited it.

The talk then turns to harassment, child safety and fraud. Harassment campaigns using AI so far look crude and draw little engagement, compared with a sophisticated pre-AI operation that abused copyright reporting against activists. Nudify apps and AI-enabled sextortion lower the effort needed, since a scammer no longer needs a genuine first image. Grossman says feared floods of synthetic abuse material into the CyberTipline have not yet materialized, though overload remains a concern for investigators.

She closes with defensive uses and dilemmas. Student-built LLM moderation bots outperformed traditional tools in a course exercise, while dual-use requests, such as a model answering questions that could help either a school administrator or an attacker, make safeguards hard to set. She urges practitioners to build the trust and safety field through peer-reviewed research and community events. The takeaway is that AI mostly makes existing harms cheaper and faster to scale.

talks.title: HIDe-&-SEEK: Who Owns Your Keyboard?
talks.teaser: Presents an open-source USB keyboard implant that logs keystrokes and relays data over a covert RF mesh for command and control.

talks.title: Becoming a Red Team Operator
talks.teaser: Explains how a penetration tester moves into full-scope red teaming, covering OPSEC, C2 choices, and reporting to blue teams.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by separating penetration testing, which tries to find as many weaknesses as possible with little concern for being noticed, from red teaming, which is organized around reaching a defined objective while staying hidden. The speaker argues that a red team must record who saw each action, from where, and when, and that a successful intrusion also exposes gaps in detection and response, not just technical flaws.

The middle of the talk covers the operator's working toolkit. Kill chain stages and MITRE ATT&CK help map activity, and the Pyramid of Pain shows how costly it is for defenders' detections to force changes in tooling. Infrastructure is the main focus: administration ports should stay closed to the internet, nginx redirectors can filter requests by path or user agent, and beacon sleep and jitter help traffic blend into normal baselines. A side-by-side capture contrasts a constant reverse shell with a Mythic agent that checks in on a schedule. Several common tools are flagged for quiet behaviour that can expose operators, including verification in TruffleHog and default checks in Pacu.

The closing section turns to reporting and collaboration. Phishing results are framed with the NIST Phish Scale, and engagement timelines and heat maps are kept in Vector so that blue teams can add their own findings. The speaker also addresses using insider knowledge fairly within a time box and treating SOC analysts as customers. The main takeaway is to keep records of failed attempts as well as successes, and to leave the defenders better prepared than before the engagement.

talks.title: EKUwu - Not Just another AD CS ESC
talks.teaser: Walks through CVE-2024-49019, where AD CS application policies in a signing request override template EKU limits.
talks.summary:
Justin Bollinger opens with a primer on Active Directory Certificate Services, likening certificate templates and signing requests to the forms and endorsements a motor vehicle agency issues. He recaps earlier research that catalogued template-based escalation paths and explains why these misconfigurations remain common in client environments.

The core of the talk follows an engagement where standard tooling reported nothing useful, but a manual look at a web server template revealed unexpected behavior. By adding extra application policies to a certificate request, the requester could push the issued certificate beyond the purpose the template allowed, including client authentication, code signing, and enrollment agent capabilities. He shows how such a certificate could be used against LDAP and Schannel to reach privileged accounts, and explains how the conflict between the standard Extended Key Usage field and Microsoft's proprietary application policies lets the requester's values prevail.

The final section covers the disclosure process with Microsoft, which initially did not treat the behavior as a vulnerability before a CVE was eventually assigned. Bollinger closes with defensive guidance: auditing template EKUs, limiting enrollment rights, requiring manager approval, monitoring issuance, and revoking suspect certificates. The takeaway for administrators is that a certificate's name and purpose need checks beyond the template alone.

talks.title: Dr. CVE Love, or how I learned to stop worrying and love vuln management
talks.teaser: Explains why raw CVE scanner output misleads, then lays out a rescoring process and metrics that focus effort on real risk.
talks.summary:
Ben Webb opens with the argument that vulnerability scanner output is mostly noise. Scanners match installed software versions against CVE databases without accounting for configuration, so backup copies and irrelevant findings inflate the totals. He argues that ranking CVEs by severity and handing lists to system owners rarely works, because the queue never empties and new issues keep arriving. He also stresses that vulnerability management cannot replace basic patching and configuration discipline, and that weak results should not be read as a judgment on the team.

The core of the talk is a four-step process. First, build an inventory of technologies with their patch cadences and a full list of scanner findings. Second, rescore those findings using threat intelligence services, which he presents as a practical way to filter out low-value items. Third, rescore again using environmental context such as subnet and business function, since the same flaw matters very differently on a shared desktop and on an isolated server. Fourth, merge the datasets, tracking when each issue was first seen. Removing items already covered by a normal patch cycle, along with findings that will never be fixed, cuts most of the volume.

What remains points to real work: systems that fall outside the patch cycle, orphaned hosts missing from asset records, and misconfigurations repeated across many machines. For reporting, he recommends trend-based KPIs such as moving averages, SLA breaches, documented exceptions, systems without a patch process, and unidentified IP addresses, rather than raw CVE totals. The practical takeaway is to choose the highest-value fix available now and accept that the work never finishes.

talks.title: Down the Rabbit Hole: Red Team Deep Fakes and the Evolution of Social Engineering
talks.teaser: Shows how red teams build deep-fake voice and video pretexts and scope realistic social-engineering tests around them.
talks.summary:
Alethe Denis, a senior security consultant on the red team at Bishop Fox, opens with a story about a real-time voice deep fake used to impersonate a chief executive and ask an employee for financial reports. She then explains the main kinds of synthetic media used in social engineering, from GAN-based video and face swapping to text-to-speech and live voice conversion, and the open-source tooling behind them. She is candid about current limits: real-time inference needs substantial GPU capacity, the delay between a spoken line and its synthetic output can expose a pretext, and video artefacts and newer platform detection features still get in the way.

The middle of the talk looks at how attackers actually use this technology. Opinion manipulation and monetised fraud dominate observed misuse, while classic intrusion sits near the bottom. She walks through the 2024 Hong Kong case, in which a finance worker was persuaded to transfer about $25 million during a video call filled with deepfaked executives. She argues that red-team scenarios often drift toward hype, and that narrow scopes and strict rules of engagement can produce a false sense of security.

Her guidance favours building scenarios from real attacker tactics and business risk, pairing a traditional red team with a deep-fake tabletop exercise, and relying on technical controls such as separation of duties and browsing restrictions alongside training. The closing questions cover verification habits, asking questions that only insiders could answer, and whether voice authentication can be trusted.

talks.title: Intelligent Response: Merging Threat Intel, MDR, and Incident Response for Maximum Impact
talks.teaser: Shows how an incident response team, MDR analysts and a threat intel lab share data to contain ransomware faster.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem that traditional incident response struggles with today's cases. Data volumes keep growing, flash storage loses deleted artifacts quickly, responder headcount is hard to scale, and ransomware groups set tight deadlines. Clients now run hybrid environments with cloud services, SaaS platforms and remote staff, so full disk collection no longer fits.

The speakers then walk through their stack. Cases are tracked in the open-source Iris platform, which is driven by its API and provisions case channels and forensic instances automatically. Velociraptor runs in containers across client environments to hunt at scale, using standardized hunts and imported offline collections. A separate MDR team works with SentinelOne and an extended detection service that ingests data from other vendors. A small group called Mixer bridges incident response and MDR, staying with a client from alert through recovery. A four-person labs team mines case data, profiles threat actors and returns new indicators and behaviors to the hunters. A Fog ransomware case shows the loop in practice: initial access through a compromised VPN and firewall vulnerabilities, credential theft, and encryption of ESXi hosts, with indicators passed to other clients within hours.

The practical takeaways are to share indicators across teams quickly, favor behavior-based detections over hash lists that attackers change, write targeted queries instead of pulling everything, and budget for storage and API rate limits at scale.

talks.title: Staunching Wounds and Staying Sane: A Survival Guide for Incident Responders
talks.teaser: Shows incident responders how to manage clients, teammates and scope using triage tactics borrowed from emergency medicine.
talks.summary:
The talk frames incident response as a customer-service role as much as a technical one, drawing parallels to emergency medicine. The speaker, an IR consultant, compares the range of cases a response team sees, from mailbox compromises and vendor-related scares to ransomware and nation-state intrusions, with the spread of patients an emergency department handles. Each case needs a different level of triage and commitment, and treating even minor callers well keeps them coming back.

Much of the practical advice centers on scoping calls, where the team learns the client's history and goals and sets realistic expectations about what can be known. The speaker covers keeping responders rested and documenting their work, staffing analysts by strengths and avoiding overload, and coordinating with threat intelligence, public relations, legal counsel, HR and recovery partners. For upset clients, the approach is to keep communication frequent, be blunt when a stressed contact is overwhelmed, and give conservative estimates, then deliver ahead of them.

On the technical side, the speaker stresses prioritizing evidence requests so that short-retention logs are not lost, avoiding rabbit holes, and isolating network segments quickly when malware is spreading, even at the cost of business downtime. Sometimes restoring operations matters more than complete forensics. The talk closes with using a painful incident to win budget for logging and tooling, plus tabletop exercises. The main takeaway is that responders cannot control attackers or client temperament, but they can manage their own team and communication.

talks.title: Worst of Cybersecurity Reporting
talks.teaser: Two reporters fact-check the most misleading security headlines of the year and show how journalists and researchers can do better.
talks.summary:
Yael Grauer and David Huerta return for their sixth annual session dissecting security and privacy news coverage from 2024. They set ground rules first: the session covers news articles rather than opinion pieces, press releases, TV segments or social media posts, and a single bad story does not mean the author or outlet is bad. Their examples are sorted into categories, running from invented claims to sensational and mistaken technical reporting.

The middle of the session walks through specific cases. A widely repeated claim about a botnet of smart toothbrushes came from a hypothetical scenario that outlets reported as fact. A story linking solar flares to a cellular outage ignored that the connection was unconfirmed, and a near-maximum CVSS score for a printer bug was presented as an apocalypse without considering how the software is deployed. Other cases include a misreading of what a Meta API could access on Netflix, the loose use of the term open source for a Llama license, and recurring myths about Signal, WhatsApp metadata, burner phones and phones secretly listening.

The closing section turns to practical advice. Journalists should push back on misleading headlines, verify claims pulled from translations or social media with the original source, and correct errors quickly. Security researchers should place severity scores in real-world context, label hypothetical examples clearly, and consult the people who would actually apply the fix. The speakers expect AI and large language models to be the next major source of misreporting.
